newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia office space is world's most costly - survey.
newsitem.headline: Asia office space is world's most costly - survey.

text.p: The world's most expensive office space is in Asia, with Tokyo the most costly, according to a survey released on Tuesday by Singapore property consultancy Edmund Tie & Company.
Asia is home to six of the 10 most expensive cities, "a reflection of the strong economic growth we have seen in the past five to 10 years", company chairman Edmund Tie told a news conference.
The Global Office Occupancy Costs Survey of 49 cities found Asia to be 95 percent more expensive on average than the United States and 57 percent dearer than Europe, the company said.
Tokyo, Hong Kong and Singapore topped the list of the world's most costly, with London fourth and Moscow fifth. Midtown New York City came in eighth.
Beijing was ranked sixth, Shanghai seventh and Taipei ninth, just ahead of Warsaw.
No Indian cities were included in the first survey because the company did not have a presence in there yet, Tie said. He said they were expected to be included in subsequent surveys.
Bombay has ranked in other surveys as the most expensive place in the world to rent office space.
This survey defined occupancy costs as a new letting of mid-floor space in prime central business locations, plus property taxes and maintenance expenses.
Conducted by Edmund Tie and its associated consultancies around the world, the survey said it cost US$12.60 per square foot per month to rent office space in Tokyo.
In second place was Hong Kong where it cost $9.78 while the same space cost $6.79 in Singapore, $5.91 in London and $4.58 in midtown New York.
The cheapest of the 49 cities was Cape Town at $0.85 per square foot per month, just behind Johannesburg at $0.89 and Auckland at $1.18.
Tie said the East-West divide would widen in the short term as Asia remained the focus of global economic expansion.
"The gap will widen further, if only slightly," he said. "The market is likely to stabilise as more of the demand is satisfied and the supply and demand imbalance is corrected."
Tie said rapid economic growth caused occupancy costs to rise as there was a lag of several years before office space supply matched demand.
"Over time, the gap between Asia and the rest of the world will narrow," Tie predicted, citing rising demand in central and eastern Europe and a growing supply of space in Asia.
Tie said political stability, telecommunications structures, quality and efficiency all had an impact on occupancy costs and the decisions companies made to establish themselves in certain cities.
He said Hong Kong would see some resurgence in rental prices because of its access to the Chinese hinterland after the handover of the territory from the British to the Chinese at the end of June.
